issues.legal_issue: The parties’ signed endorsement to an arbitral award and their later signed reaffirmation can together establish a written arbitration agreement even without a separate agreement signed before the award.
material_facts: The parties referred their disputes to an arbitrator, who made an award.
Both parties signed an endorsement stating that the award was agreed to and binding and recording their entrustment of responsibility to the arbitrator.
In a later signed letter, both parties reaffirmed the arbitrator’s appointment and agreed to abide by the award.
issues.conclusion: The parties’ written and signed conduct constituted a proper arbitration agreement, so the objection that there was no written agreement to refer the disputes to arbitration failed.
issues.legal_principle: Under section 2(a) of the Arbitration Act, 1940, the parties’ conduct and signed writings may establish an agreement in writing to refer disputes to arbitration. The Court relied on Prasun Roy v. The Calcutta Metropolitan Development Authority and Chowdhri Murtaza Hossein v. Mst. Bibi Bechunnissa.

rule.if: arbitration_award_challenge and parties_signed_award_endorsement and endorsement_recorded_agreement_to_arbitrate and parties_later_signed_reaffirmation

predicates.arbitration_award_challenge: The proceeding challenged an award made after the parties’ disputes were referred to an arbitrator.
predicates.parties_signed_award_endorsement: Both parties signed an endorsement below the award.
predicates.endorsement_recorded_agreement_to_arbitr: The signed endorsement recorded that the award was agreed to and binding and that the parties had entrusted resolution of their dispute to the arbitrator.
predicates.parties_later_signed_reaffirmation: The parties later signed a writing reaffirming the arbitrator’s appointment and agreeing to abide by the award.

issues.definition: When an award is challenged, the rule treats the parties’ signed endorsement recording their agreement to arbitrate, together with their later signed reaffirmation, as establishing a written arbitration agreement.

issues.legal_issue: A civil court may take cognizance of an award and make a decree in its terms when the dispute is civil in nature and no express or implied bar removes the court’s jurisdiction.
material_facts: An application was made to file the award and obtain judgment in its terms under sections 14 and 17 of the Arbitration Act, 1940.
The trial court made a decree in terms of the award.
The petitioner argued that the earlier proceedings were without jurisdiction.
The Court found no express or implied prohibition on the civil court taking cognizance of the award and no inability of the judge to hear the matter.
issues.conclusion: The civil court had jurisdiction to take cognizance of the award, and the contention that the previous proceedings were without jurisdiction failed.
issues.legal_principle: Section 9 of the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908, gives courts jurisdiction over suits of a civil nature unless cognizance is expressly or impliedly barred. Sections 14 and 17 of the Arbitration Act, 1940, provide for the court’s role concerning an award. The Court relied on Rajah Amir Hassan Khan v. Sheo Baksh Singh, Seth Hira Lal Patni v. Shri Kali Nath, and Vasudev Dhanjibhai Modi v. Rajabhai Abdul Rehman, including the principle that a decree may be challenged for want of inherent jurisdiction only where the court lacked jurisdiction over the subject matter or parties, or was otherwise entirely without jurisdiction.

rule.if: civil_award_filing_proceeding and civil_nature_dispute and no_express_or_implied_cognizance_bar and court_inherent_capacity

predicates.civil_award_filing_proceeding: The proceeding asked a civil court to take cognizance of an award and give effect to it.
predicates.civil_nature_dispute: The underlying dispute was civil in nature.
predicates.no_express_or_implied_cognizance_bar: No express or implied rule barred the court from taking cognizance of the proceeding.
predicates.court_inherent_capacity: The court was not inherently incapable of deciding the matter and had jurisdiction over the dispute and the parties.

issues.definition: The rule means that a civil court has jurisdiction over an award proceeding when the proceeding concerns a civil dispute, no rule bars the court from hearing it, and the court is not inherently incapable of deciding it.

issues.legal_issue: A challenge to an award decree is barred by res judicata when the same disputes have already been raised in prior proceedings before a court with jurisdiction and the resulting decree has become final.
material_facts: The petitioner challenged the decree in an appeal and a revision, then withdrew both after an agreement reaffirming the award; the trial court’s decree consequently became final.
The petitioner later brought a suit to set aside the decree and withdrew the appeal or revision arising from that matter.
During execution, the petitioner again raised substantially the same disputes in a revision application.
The High Court held that the revision was barred by res judicata, and the Supreme Court upheld that conclusion.
issues.conclusion: The High Court was right to hold that the revision was barred by res judicata.
issues.legal_principle: The Court applied the principle of res judicata and relied on Rajah Amir Hassan Khan v. Sheo Baksh Singh for the rule that a court with jurisdiction to decide an issue does not lose that jurisdiction merely because its decision may have been wrong. It also relied on Seth Hira Lal Patni v. Shri Kali Nath and Vasudev Dhanjibhai Modi v. Rajabhai Abdul Rehman concerning when a decree may be attacked for inherent lack of jurisdiction.

rule.if: execution_or_revision_challenging_award_decree and same_disputes_raised_in_prior_proceedings and prior_decree_became_final and prior_court_had_jurisdiction

predicates.execution_or_revision_challenging_award_: The proceeding was an execution-related or revisional challenge to a decree giving effect to an award.
predicates.same_disputes_raised_in_prior_proceeding: The challenger had already raised substantially the same disputes in earlier proceedings.
predicates.prior_decree_became_final: The earlier proceedings ended with the decree becoming final.
predicates.prior_court_had_jurisdiction: The court in the earlier proceedings had jurisdiction to decide the matter.

issues.definition: The rule means that a repeat challenge to an award decree is barred when the same disputes were raised in earlier proceedings, the decree became final, and the earlier court had jurisdiction.
